_: Первый ролик канала. Тема: крушение бронзового века около 1200 года до нашей эры. Выбрана намеренно: она держится на атмосфере и на честной неопределённости, а не на сенсации, и под неё есть настоящий материал в открытых архивах — Мединет-Абу, Угарит, Микены, Хаттуса, Амарнские письма.

_цветокор: Бронза на морозе: синяя тень и бронзовые света. Ролик про металл, который дал веку имя, и про ночь, в которую он кончился. Архивная — цианотипия: этим синим отпечатком печатали планы раскопов.
script_blocks: There is a letter that was never delivered. It was written on a clay tablet in a city on the coast of what is now northern Syria, in a kingdom called Ugarit, a little after twelve hundred BC. The king writes to a neighbour, and the tone is not the tone kings usually use. He says that ships have been seen. He says that his own fleet is away, in the waters off another country, and his troops are away as well, in the land of the Hittites, and that his city is therefore open. Whatever comes, he says, will find nobody at the gates. The tablet was found in the ruins of the building where it was written, in an oven, waiting to be fired hard enough to travel. It never left. The city burned before the letter could be baked, and the fire that destroyed Ugarit did the one thing that could preserve that clay for three thousand years. This is how we know. Not from a chronicle written afterwards by somebody who survived, because there is no such chronicle. We know because a message about the end was still sitting in the kiln when the end arrived. Tonight I want to tell you about the years around that letter. Not as a disaster story, and not as a mystery with a neat solution at the end, because there is not one. I want to tell you what the world looked like before it stopped, what actually happened as far as anyone can establish it, and why a collapse that took place over roughly half a century still gets argued about in every generation of scholarship since. Settle in. This one takes its time. Before we go further, one thing about the way this video is put together. I am not going to give you a villain. Every popular account of this period reaches for one, because a collapse with a culprit is easier to hold in your head than a collapse with six overlapping causes, and for most of the twentieth century the culprit was a mysterious sea-borne enemy that arrived from nowhere and burned everything. That story is still repeated. It is built on one temple inscription and a great deal of imagination, and the evidence for it has been getting weaker for forty years while the evidence for something slower and stranger has been getting stronger. So there will be no single answer here. What there will be is a set of things we can actually demonstrate, laid next to each other in the order they seem to have happened, and an honest account of where the joins are.

To understand what was lost you have to understand how connected that world was, because the usual picture of the ancient world is wrong in exactly the way that matters. We tend to imagine isolated kingdoms, each in its own valley, meeting mainly to fight. The late bronze age was not that. For roughly three hundred years, from about the fifteenth century to the beginning of the twelfth, the eastern Mediterranean ran as something close to a single system. Egypt in the south. The Hittite empire across Anatolia. Assyria and Babylon in the east. The Mycenaean palaces in Greece. Cyprus in the middle of it all, with its copper. And along the Levantine coast a string of harbour cities, Ugarit the richest of them, whose whole existence was the movement of goods between the others. These were not vague trading contacts. They were formal, regulated, and written down. Kings addressed each other as brother. They exchanged gifts on a schedule, married each other's daughters, sent doctors and craftsmen back and forth on request, and complained bitterly in writing when a shipment arrived light. There were treaties with clauses about extradition. There was, in effect, a shared diplomatic language, and it was Akkadian, which by then was nobody's mother tongue in most of these courts. It was the Latin of its day, learned by scribes so that a scribe in Egypt could write something a scribe in Anatolia could read. When I say the bronze age collapsed, that is the thing that collapsed. Not a country. A network. There is a particular find that makes all of this physical, and it sits at the bottom of the sea off the southern coast of Turkey, at a place called Uluburun. A sponge diver noticed metal shapes on the seabed in the nineteen eighties. What was raised over the following decade was a ship that sank around thirteen hundred BC with its cargo still aboard, and the cargo is the age in miniature. Ten tonnes of copper in ingots shaped like ox hides. A tonne of tin, in roughly the right proportion to alloy the whole lot into bronze. Glass ingots the colour of cobalt. Ebony from Africa. Ivory. Terebinth resin in Canaanite jars. Ostrich eggshells. Gold and silver jewellery, a gold scarab bearing the name of Nefertiti, weights in at least two different regional standards, and, in the personal possessions of the crew, objects from Mycenaean Greece. One ship, one voyage, and material from at least seven cultures on board. Whatever else the late bronze age was, it was not a collection of isolated worlds.

The name of the age is also its weakness, and this is the part that most retellings skip past. Bronze is not a metal you find. It is a metal you make, by alloying copper with tin, roughly nine parts to one. Copper was awkward but manageable, because there was a great deal of it on Cyprus, and Cyprus sat in the middle of the sea lanes. Tin was the problem. There is almost no tin in the eastern Mediterranean. The nearest sources of any size were far to the east, in what is now Afghanistan, and far to the west, in Cornwall and Brittany. Either way, every ingot of tin that reached a bronze workshop in Greece or Egypt had crossed thousands of kilometres, through many hands, along routes that no single kingdom controlled. Think about what that means. The defining material of the age, the material used for weapons, for armour, for tools, for ploughshares and sickles and the fittings of chariots, could not be produced by any of the great powers on their own. Every one of them depended on a supply chain that ran through territory belonging to somebody else. In good years this was invisible, the way infrastructure always is. It only becomes visible when it stops. And a system in which everybody depends on everybody has a property that looks like strength right up until the moment it becomes the opposite: it transmits failure as efficiently as it transmits goods. There is a second fragility that gets less attention, and it is not about metal at all. These were palace economies, which means the state did not tax a market: the state was the market. Grain came in to the palace and went out again by decision. Craftsmen were on rations. Land was allocated and recorded. That arrangement is enormously efficient when it works, because it lets a kingdom concentrate resources on chariots, walls and temples faster than any looser system could. It also has no redundancy. There is no independent merchant class holding stock, no second network of private storage to fall back on, no way for the countryside to reorganise distribution on its own if the centre stops issuing. Every family fed by the palace was fed by a single institution, and the institution kept its records in one building. Concentration of that kind always looks like strength from inside. It is only afterwards, from the outside, that it looks like a single point of failure.

We know the tone of that world better than we know almost anything else about it, because of an accident in Egypt. Late in the fourteenth century BC the pharaoh Akhenaten moved his capital to a new site in the desert, a place we call Amarna. The city was occupied for a little over a decade and then abandoned, and because it was abandoned rather than rebuilt, the rubbish stayed where it fell. In the eighteen eighties a local woman digging for fertiliser found clay tablets in the ruins. Around three hundred and eighty of them have been recovered since. They are the diplomatic correspondence of the Egyptian court, and reading them is a strange experience, because the voices are so immediate. A king of Babylon complains that the gold sent from Egypt was not what was promised, that when he put it in the furnace it did not come out as it should have. Another writes that he heard the pharaoh held a festival and did not invite him. There are letters from small vassal rulers in the Levant, sending greetings in the most elaborate terms and then, in the last few lines, asking for archers, because the situation is deteriorating and nobody has come. Some of those letters were answered. Some clearly were not. What comes through, across three thousand years, is not the grandeur of empires. It is the ordinary texture of a functioning international system, with all its pettiness, and the assumption, running under every line, that there will be a next letter. One correspondence in that archive is worth singling out, because it shows how the system behaved when it was already under strain. A ruler in the Levantine hills writes again and again to Egypt. He reports that the countryside is slipping out of control, that towns have gone over to a group he calls the habiru, and that unless troops are sent the whole district will be lost. He is a loyal vassal, he says, and he has written before. He writes again. Modern readers have spilled a great deal of ink on who the habiru were, and the current view is that they were not an ethnic group at all but a social category: people who had left the settled order and lived outside it, brigands, refugees, mercenaries, depending on the year. That is the detail I want you to keep. Two generations before the collapse, in the middle of the golden age, there were already people falling out of the bottom of this society in numbers large enough to be a military problem, and the imperial answer was mostly silence.

So let us go back to Ugarit, because Ugarit is where the ending is documented most closely. The city stood a few kilometres from the sea, with its own harbour town, and it was rich in the particular way that middlemen are rich. It sat between the Hittite empire, to whom it paid tribute, and Egypt, with whom it traded, and it grew fat on the traffic. The palace had a scriptorium. Merchants there kept accounts in several languages. And someone in that city, at some point in the thirteenth century, did something quietly extraordinary: they wrote their own language, a Semitic language we now call Ugaritic, using a cuneiform script cut down to about thirty signs. Thirty. Not several hundred. It is one of the earliest alphabets we have. The last layer of the city tells the rest. Arrowheads in the streets. Destruction by fire, thorough enough that the walls came down. And in the ruins, tablets, including the letter I began with and several others in the same register. One reports that the enemy ships have already burned towns. Another, from the Hittite side, orders grain to be sent urgently and asks whether it has arrived, because there is famine. After that, nothing. The site was not rebuilt. A city that had existed for centuries, at one of the best harbours on that coast, simply stopped being a place where people lived. The archives of Ugarit deserve a moment on their own, because of what survives in them beside the letters. There are legal documents about inheritance and debt. There are lists of ships and their owners. There are records of a merchant class wealthy enough to lend to the palace. And there is literature: long poems about gods and kings, written down in that thirty-sign alphabet, which have shaped how scholars read the religious language of the whole region ever since. A city that we would otherwise know only as a name on a map turns out to have had a literature, a legal system, a mixed economy and several working languages. Now hold that beside the archaeology. Above the destruction layer at Ugarit there is nothing. Not a poorer town, not a squatter occupation of the ruins, not a later village on the mound. The site was simply left, and the harbour that had served ships for centuries stood empty, and everything I have just listed stopped existing within the span of a single season.

Now the part everybody has heard of, and the part that most needs care. In Egypt, on the wall of a mortuary temple at Medinet Habu, the pharaoh Ramesses the third left an account of fighting in the eighth year of his reign, around eleven seventy-seven BC. The reliefs show a land battle and a sea battle. The text says that foreign lands made a conspiracy in their islands, that no land could stand before their arms, and it lists places that had already fallen, the Hittite lands among them. It names the attackers. The names are transliterated in various ways, and you may have seen them: Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen, Weshesh, Sherden. Modern books group them under a term the Egyptians never used, invented in the nineteenth century by a French Egyptologist: the Sea Peoples. That phrase has done a great deal of harm, because it sounds like the name of a nation. It is not. It is a modern label for a list of names in one propaganda inscription, carved on a temple wall by the side that says it won, describing enemies it may have had every reason to describe as more numerous and more terrible than they were. What the inscription shows is real. It shows ships with bird-head prows, and warriors in feathered or reed headdresses, and, in the land scenes, ox carts carrying women and children. Not a raid. A movement of people. But that is what one Egyptian relief shows. It is evidence. It is not an explanation, and for a long time it was treated as one. It is also worth looking at the reliefs the way an editor would rather than the way a tourist does. Egyptian temple art is not reportage. It is an official statement in a fixed visual language, carved to be seen by gods and by future kings, and its rules are older than the events it shows. Pharaoh is always enormous. Enemies are always in disarray. The outcome is always total. Ramesses the third had a further reason to make the claim vast: he was consciously modelling himself on Ramesses the second, and a great victory over a great enemy was part of the costume. None of this means the fighting is invented. There is other evidence that something serious arrived at Egypt's borders in these decades, and the detail in the ships is too specific to be decorative invention. It means that the scale, the unity and the menace of the enemy are exactly the parts of the picture we should trust least, because they are exactly the parts the medium was built to exaggerate.

It is worth being precise about what we do not know here, because that precision is the whole difference between history and a story that merely sounds good. We do not know where these groups came from. Various origins have been argued from the name forms alone, and name forms are treacherous. We do not know whether they were a coordinated alliance or several unrelated movements that Egyptian scribes lumped together because they arrived in the same decades. We do not know whether they were the cause of the collapse, a symptom of it, or both in different places, and there is a serious case for the middle option: that these were people already displaced by whatever was happening elsewhere, moving because staying had become impossible. Some of them settled. The Peleset are generally identified with the Philistines, who appear shortly afterwards in the southern Levant with distinctive pottery that has clear Aegean features, then, over the following century, gradually stop making it and adopt local styles instead. That is not the archaeology of an invincible horde. It is the archaeology of migrants who arrive, hold on to what they brought, and are slowly absorbed. Here is the difficulty in one sentence: if migrating groups brought down the whole system, something must explain why so many groups were on the move at once, and that something has to be found elsewhere. There is one more reason to be careful with the invasion story, and it is a matter of arithmetic. Moving people by sea in the twelfth century BC was hard. The ships of the period carried tens of tonnes, not hundreds; they sailed in season, hugged coasts where they could, and needed water and food from land at intervals. A force large enough to destroy a fortified palace centre had to be fed on the way there, and a migration large enough to displace whole populations needed somewhere to have come from. Both requirements point at the same awkward question. If the raiders were numerous, what was feeding them, in a decade when the letters are full of famine? The likelier reading is that the movements were smaller than the inscriptions suggest, and that they arrived at places already weakened from within: not an army knocking down a healthy city, but groups pushing at doors that had already come off their hinges.

The most serious candidate for that something is the weather, and the evidence for it does not come from any text. It comes from mud, and from the shells of tiny organisms, and it has only become good in the last twenty years or so. Pollen cores taken from lake beds and lagoons in the Levant and in Anatolia preserve a record of what was growing nearby, year by year. Read down through those layers and you can see the vegetation change. Around the end of the thirteenth century and into the twelfth, the signal in several of these cores shifts in the same direction: fewer of the trees that need water, more of the plants that tolerate dryness. Isotope work on sediments in the eastern Mediterranean points the same way, towards cooler sea surface temperatures and reduced rainfall. The picture that emerges is a dry phase lasting decades, not a single failed harvest. And now put that next to the texts, which were written by people who had no idea what a pollen core was. The Hittite king writes to Ugarit about grain, and calls it a matter of life or death. An Egyptian record mentions grain sent to keep the Hittite land alive. A letter speaks of famine in the house of a ruler. These are not literary laments. They are logistics, and they are urgent, and they line up in time with the mud. Two things about the drought evidence are worth saying plainly, because this is where popular retellings usually overreach. The first is that climate proxies are blunt about timing. A pollen core can show you a dry phase across a few decades; it cannot tell you which harvest failed, and the dating comes with error bars measured in decades rather than years. So the honest claim is that a sustained dry period overlaps the collapse in time, not that a particular drought caused a particular destruction. The second is that drought alone does not end civilisations. This region had dry decades before and after, and got through them. What makes this one different is what it landed on: an interlocking system with no slack in it, where the state was the only distributor of food, where the armies were expensive, and where the neighbours who might have sent grain were having the same weather at the same time. Drought is not the answer. It is the first push.

Then there is the ground itself, and this is where I want to be careful, because it is the explanation people find most satisfying and it is the weakest of the strong ones. Many of the great sites destroyed in this period show damage consistent with earthquakes: walls fallen in one direction, columns dropped in place, bodies found under collapse rather than in graves. Some archaeologists have argued for what is called an earthquake storm, a sequence of major quakes along connected fault systems over a few decades, of the sort that has been documented in Anatolia in modern times. It is plausible. The region is seismically violent and always has been. But two things restrain it. First, earthquake damage and destruction by fire and violence are genuinely hard to tell apart in a burnt layer three thousand years old, and the interpretation often depends on how the excavator read the debris. Second, and more decisively, these societies had survived earthquakes for centuries. Cities in this region fell down and were rebuilt as a matter of routine. What needs explaining is not why buildings collapsed. It is why, this time, they were not put back up. A society with functioning agriculture, functioning trade and functioning administration rebuilds after an earthquake. A society that has lost those things does not, and the earthquake merely decides which year the abandonment happens. There is a variant of this argument that I do find persuasive, and it is narrower. Whether or not there was an unusual sequence of earthquakes, a single ordinary one arriving at the wrong moment can be decisive for a society already running on empty. Rebuilding a palace takes surplus, organised labour and time, and all three of those are the first things a hungry state runs out of. So the earthquake stops being a cause and becomes a trigger: the event that converts a slow decline into an abandonment, and fixes the date at which a place stops appearing in the record. That is a much smaller claim than the one usually made, and it sits comfortably beside everything else in this video. It also explains something otherwise odd about the archaeology, which is that the destructions are not simultaneous. They are spread across decades, in different regions, in an order that no single invading force could produce, and each one looks locally like the end of the world.

Which brings us to the explanation that has slowly won, and it is the least dramatic one available. It has a dry name: systems collapse. The idea is that no single cause was sufficient, and that looking for one is the mistake. Instead, several pressures arrived within the same few decades, and the network that had made everyone wealthy turned out to be the thing that spread the damage. Follow it through. A long dry phase reduces harvests across a wide region. Reduced harvests mean less surplus, and in these societies surplus is not luxury, it is the entire basis of the state, because the palace collects grain, stores it, and redistributes it. Less surplus means less to trade, and less to pay soldiers and officials with. Trade routes become less safe, partly because there is more banditry and piracy when people are hungry, partly because fewer ships are sailing to keep them familiar. Less trade means less tin, and less tin means the bronze economy itself begins to falter. Hungry populations move. Moving populations put pressure on places that are already short. Kingdoms under pressure stop being able to send help to neighbours, so the letters asking for grain go unanswered, and the network that once transmitted goods now transmits nothing but failure. Each step is modest. It is the sequence that is fatal. I want to make one part of that chain concrete, because it is the part people find hardest to believe. Why would trade stop simply because harvests were bad? Because long-distance trade in this world was not a market responding to demand. It was carried out by ships and caravans financed by palaces and by a small number of merchant houses, insured by nothing, and dependent on the certainty that at the far end there would be a functioning port with an official who honoured the agreement. Remove two or three ports from that chain and the voyage no longer has a reason to exist, because there is nobody to sell to and nowhere safe to shelter halfway. Trade of this kind does not decline gently in proportion to conditions. It works, and then at some point it is not worth the risk, and then it does not work at all. Networks fail the way ropes fail: not fibre by fibre in a smooth curve, but slowly and then suddenly.

You can watch this happen in Greece, and the Greek case has a detail that makes the whole argument concrete. The Mycenaean palaces, Mycenae itself, Pylos, Tiryns, Thebes, were not primarily fortresses or royal residences, though they were those things too. They were administrative machines. We know this because their record-keeping survived, again by fire, in the same accidental way: clay tablets written in the script we call Linear B, baked hard by the flames that destroyed the buildings they were stored in. And when Linear B was deciphered in the nineteen fifties, the content came as a disappointment to anyone hoping for poetry. There is no poetry. There are inventories. Numbers of sheep, by flock and by shepherd. Quantities of grain issued. Bronze allocated to named smiths, in weights so precise that in one case the amount recorded is too small to make anything much at all, which some read as evidence that metal had become scarce enough to count carefully. Lists of people and their rations. This was a palace economy: goods flowed in, were recorded, and flowed out again by decision. Which means that when the palace burned, the accounting burned with it, and there was no market in the modern sense to take over the work of distribution. The result was not merely political change. Within two generations, writing itself disappears from Greece, and it does not return for something like four hundred years. There is a detail from Pylos that I have never been able to forget. Among the last tablets written there, in what appears to be the final period before the palace burned, are texts recording the posting of watchers to the coast, and an unusual religious offering, a list of gifts to a number of deities that reads as if someone were trying everything at once. The cautious reading is that we do not know what these documents mean; the temptation to hear panic in them is obvious and should be resisted. But the plainer point stands and does not depend on interpretation. The last thing that palace did, as far as we can tell, was administration: somebody was still recording, still filing, still doing the job. And then the building burned so thoroughly that the clay in the archive room was fired to the hardness of pottery, which is why we can read any of it at all. Every one of these archives is a gift from the fire that destroyed the place that made it.

The Hittite ending is stranger, and quieter, and to my mind the most haunting of them all. Hattusa, the capital, stood on a high plateau in central Anatolia, a city of temples and archives behind walls with gate figures of lions and sphinxes. It was, on any measure, one of the great powers, a state that had fought Egypt to a standstill at Kadesh and then signed a treaty with it, a copy of which hangs today at the United Nations. And around twelve hundred BC, Hattusa stops. There is destruction at the site. But excavation has suggested something that no invasion explains: parts of the city appear to have been emptied deliberately before the end. Valuables removed. Archives partly cleared. Some buildings apparently stripped and then closed up, in the manner of an evacuation rather than a sack. Whoever burned Hattusa may have burned a city that had already been substantially abandoned by the people who ran it. Picture that. Not a night of fire and screaming, but carts leaving over months, and offices closing one after another, and a decision taken somewhere that the capital of an empire was no longer a place that could be held. Where they went, we do not know. Small successor kingdoms in the south and east carried the Hittite name and language forward for centuries, which suggests that the people did not vanish. The state did. The Hittite case also gives us the clearest surviving voice of the crisis, and it is not about armies. In the final decades, Hittite correspondence is preoccupied with grain: where it is, whose ships are carrying it, whether it has arrived. One letter refers to a shipment as a matter of life and death, in those words. The empire that had fought Egypt to a draw was, at the end, importing food through the ports of a vassal kingdom on the Syrian coast, and that vassal kingdom was Ugarit, whose own last letters are about ships and fire. When Ugarit stopped, the Hittite supply line stopped with it. You can see the whole logic of the collapse in that single dependency: a landlocked empire on a dry plateau, feeding itself through one coastal city, in a decade when the coast was the least safe place in the world. Neither of them was destroyed by the other's fall. They simply could not survive it separately.

Egypt survived, and how it survived is instructive, because survival is not the same as coming through unharmed. Ramesses the third held the Delta, and the reliefs at Medinet Habu record it in the language of total victory. Egypt was better placed than anyone: agriculture that depended on the Nile flood rather than on rainfall, a unified administration, and depth to fall back into. But look at what happens next. Within about thirty years of that celebrated victory, we have records of the first documented labour strike in history, at Deir el-Medina, the village of the workmen who cut the royal tombs. They downed tools and sat outside the mortuary temples because their grain rations had not arrived on time. These were not marginal people. They were skilled state employees, the most reliably paid workers in the country, and the state could not feed them on schedule. There are also records of a conspiracy inside the royal household against Ramesses himself, and the trial documents survive. Within a century, effective control of the country had divided, with the priesthood of Amun at Thebes holding the south in practice while pharaohs ruled from the north. Egypt did not fall. Egypt spent the following centuries as a smaller, poorer, more inward country than the one that had traded with the whole eastern Mediterranean, and it never fully returned to that world, because that world was gone. There is a document from the end of this Egyptian decline that says more than any inscription. It is a report, written in the eleventh century, by an official named Wenamun, sent from Thebes up the coast to buy timber for a sacred boat. In the older world this would have been a formality: an Egyptian envoy arrives, the local ruler provides. Instead he is robbed at one port, kept waiting for weeks at another, and finally told by the prince of Byblos, in as many words, that he is not the servant of Egypt and that timber will be supplied when payment is supplied. The envoy has to send home for goods. He is lectured on the shortness of his own king's reach. Whether the text is an official account or a literary work built on one, its assumptions are the point: everyone reading it knew that this was now how the world worked. Two centuries earlier that conversation could not have happened. The empire had not fallen. It had simply stopped being obeyed.

It is worth pausing here to say what did not happen, because the phrase dark age carries more than it should. People did not disappear. The eastern Mediterranean was not empty in the twelfth and eleventh centuries; villages continued, fields were worked, pots were made, children were born and buried with small offerings. What ended was the top layer: the palaces, the scribes, the long-distance trade in luxuries, the diplomatic marriages, the monumental building. Those are exactly the things that leave the most visible traces, so their absence looks, in the archaeological record, like the absence of everything. It is not. It is the absence of the parts that were written down. And in some places, life after the palaces was measurably better for the people at the bottom. Studies of skeletal remains from certain post-palatial sites suggest populations that were, on some measures, no worse nourished than before, and sometimes better. This makes sense if you think about who the palace system was for. A palace economy takes in grain and metal from the countryside and redistributes it according to the palace's priorities, and when it stops, the countryside keeps what it grows. There is a real loss in complexity, in literacy, in art, in ambition. It is not the same as a loss for every person alive, and being honest about that difference is part of taking the period seriously. It is also worth noticing which regions did comparatively well, because the pattern is consistent and it tells you what the collapse actually targeted. The places that suffered least were the ones least integrated into the palace system: coastal towns with mixed economies, inland villages that had always fed themselves, islands with fishing and small trade. The places that suffered most were the great administrative centres, the ones with the most impressive walls, the largest archives and the widest trading reach. Complexity was not protection. It was exposure. That is an uncomfortable thing to sit with, and I am not going to draw a modern moral out of it, because the differences between then and now are at least as important as the similarities. But it is the finding, and it has been arrived at independently by people studying collapses in places and periods that have nothing else in common.

And out of that gap came the things the next age was built on, which is the part of the story I find hardest to hold in my head. The alphabet, which had been invented earlier and used in the margins by merchants and at Ugarit, comes into its own. Phoenician cities on the same coast, less damaged than their neighbours, take up long-distance trade again, and their script is portable in a way that cuneiform and Linear B never were: a couple of dozen signs that a merchant can learn in a season, rather than hundreds that require a scribal school and a decade. Almost every alphabet in use in the world tonight, including the letters you would be reading if you were reading rather than listening, descends from that one. Iron spreads, not because it is a better metal than bronze at first, because early iron is not, but because iron ore is common and local, and after the collapse the tin route was gone. A material that any region could obtain replaced a material that required an international system. And in Greece, four centuries later, when writing returns in an alphabet borrowed from those same Phoenicians, one of the first things put into it is a poem about a war against a city in Anatolia, fought by kings from palaces that had by then been ruins for longer than the poem's audience could imagine. Homer's world is a memory of the world that ended here, remembered by people who no longer knew what it had been. The other inheritance is harder to see and probably matters more. When the palaces went, so did the idea that writing belonged to a professional class employed by the state. Linear B was a tool for accountants working for a king; there is no private letter in the entire corpus, no poem, no contract between two ordinary people. The alphabet that spread afterwards was different in kind, not just in efficiency. It could be learned informally, used for trade, for law, for verse, for graffiti scratched on a cup. Some of the earliest Greek alphabetic writing we have is exactly that: a line of playful verse on a wine jug. Within a few centuries the same script is carrying legal codes posted in public where citizens can read them, which is an idea with consequences. It is not that the collapse produced these things. It is that the thing standing in their way was removed, and it was removed by the disaster.

So what do we actually know, when the arguing stops? We know that between roughly twelve hundred and eleven fifty BC, a large number of cities across the eastern Mediterranean were destroyed or abandoned within the span of a few decades. We know the network that connected them ended, and did not come back in the same form. We know there was drought, because the mud says so. We know there was famine, because the letters say so. We know there were movements of people, because Egypt recorded them and the pottery of the southern Levant confirms that some of them settled. We know that Greece lost writing for four centuries, that the Hittite state ceased to exist, and that Egypt survived diminished. What we do not know is the order of operations. Which pressure came first in any given place, how much each contributed, and whether the same explanation holds for Pylos and for Ugarit, six hundred kilometres and a different world apart. New evidence keeps arriving and keeps complicating the picture rather than simplifying it, which is what good evidence usually does. If you take one thing from tonight, I would like it to be that: not a solved mystery, but a well-documented uncertainty, which is a rarer and more valuable thing. I should be honest about how the field itself has moved, because that is part of the evidence too. For most of the twentieth century the invasion explanation was standard, and it was standard partly because the excavators of the period were reading their burnt layers with Homer and the Egyptian reliefs in hand. Then radiocarbon dating improved, and the destructions turned out to be spread over decades rather than clustered in one year. Then the climate proxies arrived, and a dry phase appeared that nobody had known about. Then the tablets from the last years of Ugarit and Hattusa were read properly, and turned out to be about grain rather than glory. Each of these arrivals made the story less dramatic and more convincing. That is usually the direction good evidence pushes, and it is worth remembering the next time anyone offers you a clean single cause for anything that happened three thousand years ago.

There is one last image I want to leave you with, and then I will let you sleep. Somewhere in the ruins of Ugarit, in a room off a courtyard, there was an oven with tablets inside it. Somebody had written them, and stacked them, and lit the fire, and then something happened that meant nobody came back to take them out. We do not know that person's name. We do not know whether they got out of the city, or whether they were still nearby when the roof came down. What we know is that the last thing they did at work was ordinary. Fire the tablets. Send the letters. Deal with the ships in the morning. That is what the end of an age looks like from the inside: not a curtain coming down, but a normal afternoon that turns out to have been the last one, in a job that will not exist next year, in a city that has perhaps two more weeks. Everyone in this story thought they were living in the middle of something. Their world had lasted three centuries and had every appearance of permanence, with its treaties and its shipping lanes and its shared professional language, and it took about fifty years to stop. The clay outlasted all of it. And there is a last thing, which is the reason I wanted to start this channel with this story rather than with something more famous. We have the letters from Ugarit and the tablets from Pylos and the archive at Hattusa for exactly one reason: those places burned. Every archive we can read from this world is an archive that was baked by the fire that ended it. The cities that declined slowly, that were tidied up and abandoned in good order, left us almost nothing, because unfired clay dissolves back into mud within a season of rain. So our picture of the collapse is assembled, necessarily, out of its most violent moments, and the quiet endings, which were probably the more common kind, are simply missing. Keep that in mind whenever anyone tells you what the ancient world was like. We are not looking at the past. We are looking at the small part of it that happened to be set on fire at the right moment, and read it as well as we can. Thank you for listening. If these long, quiet histories are the kind of thing you want more of, the channel is here, and there will be another one. Sleep well.

youtube.title: The Letter That Was Never Sent: How the Bronze Age Ended
title_alternatives: 1177 BC: The Year the Ancient World Stopped Working
The Collapse of the Bronze Age, Told Slowly
youtube.description_intro: A little after 1200 BC, a king on the Syrian coast wrote a letter saying that ships had been seen and his city was undefended. The letter was still in the kiln when the city burned, which is why we can read it today. Over the following decades the entire connected world of the eastern Mediterranean came apart: Ugarit, Mycenae, Hattusa. Egypt survived, diminished. This is what actually happened, what the evidence really shows, and why the question is still open.

youtube.description_notes: A general interest documentary made for slow evening listening. Dates follow the conventional chronology and are given as they are currently understood; where specialists disagree, the video says so rather than choosing for you. Nothing here is settled, and that is the interesting part.
